name: Leaders Who Model Use
title: Leaders Who Model Use
answer: Leaders who model AI use show staff that AI is a normal tool with real limits, not something reserved for other people. When leaders follow the same rules they set, staff take those rules seriously. Modeling also includes admitting uncertainty, which makes it safe for staff to experiment and share failures.

sections.body: This idea is about leaders demonstrating AI use rather than only talking about it. Staff pay more attention to what leaders do than to what they say, so a superintendent who never uses AI while asking teachers to use it signals that AI is for other people. A principal who shares how they drafted a newsletter with AI, and what needed fixing, presents AI as an ordinary tool with genuine limits. This builds credibility and makes the recommended habits feel real rather than imposed.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school or classroom, leaders model the same habits the book recommends for everyone. They remove names before using a general tool, check every fact, and keep decisions human. When leaders follow the rules they set, staff take those rules seriously, and when leaders cut corners, staff notice. Modeling also means admitting uncertainty, so leaders do not need to be AI experts. They need to be curious, honest about what they do not know, and willing to learn alongside staff, which makes it safe for staff to experiment and share what goes wrong.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no study, figure or finding for this idea. It rests on practice and observation rather than research, describing how staff watch leaders and what that means for credibility and rule-following.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits and risks sit in the gap between what leaders say and what they do. A leader who asks others to use AI but never uses it sends the message that AI is for other people. A leader who cuts corners on the recommended habits, such as removing names, checking facts, or keeping decisions human, will be noticed by staff. The decisions that stay with a person include how to use AI, what to fix in its output, and which decisions remain human. Leaders are also expected to be honest about what they do not know rather than pretending to be experts.
